analysis.one_liner: Bans campaign money from U.S. corporations owned or controlled by foreign nationals.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Administration Committee and received no vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill extends the existing ban on foreign nationals giving or spending money in U.S. elections to American companies that are owned or steered by foreign nationals, defining those companies by specific ownership thresholds (such as 20% or more foreign voting shares) and by whether foreigners can dictate the company's political decisions [S3]. Before any corporation spends money in a federal election, its CEO would have to certify under penalty of perjury that the company is not foreign-controlled, and corporate political action committees would have to certify that no foreign national participates in or influences their decisions [S3]. It would also make clear that political committees may not take disbursements from companies that dodge the rules, or from committees themselves accepting non-compliant money [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: American voters, who would gain clearer assurance that federal election spending by corporations reflects U.S. ownership and control rather than foreign national influence. The bill would also put the onus on corporate executives, who must certify compliance under penalty of perjury, creating a personal legal deterrent [S3]. Ordinary citizens cannot legally funnel money into U.S. federal elections through foreign-controlled corporate shells under this bill, closing a channel the current law leaves open for domestic companies that are foreign-owned or foreign-directed [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: American voters against foreign election influence

how_it_helps.text: Extends the existing foreign-national spending ban to any U.S. corporation, LLC, or partnership that is foreign-controlled, foreign-influenced, or foreign-owned — defined with specific tests like 5% or 20% foreign voting ownership, joint foreign control of 50% or more, or foreign power to dictate company decisions — closing a gap in current law [S3].

Requires a company's chief executive to certify under penalty of perjury, before the company spends money in a federal election, that it is not prohibited from doing so, putting personal legal accountability behind the ban [S3].

Bars corporate PACs from contributing unless they certify that no foreign national participates in or influences the fund's decisions, and that any foreign directors abstain from votes about the fund [S3].
Blocks disbursements to political committees that accept donations outside the Federal Election Campaign Act's limits and reporting rules, cutting off a laundering route for non-compliant money [S2].

analysis.who_pays: U.S. corporations with significant foreign ownership or foreign influence would lose the ability to make campaign contributions and expenditures, and would bear new compliance costs: annual CEO certifications under penalty of perjury and, for corporate PACs, certifications about fund management and foreign-director abstentions [S3]. Companies with borderline foreign ownership would face uncertainty in determining whether the thresholds apply to them [S3].

drawbacks.text: The annual CEO certification creates a compliance burden and legal exposure for corporate executives, and companies near the ownership thresholds (5% or 20% foreign voting shares) would face real uncertainty about whether they qualify as foreign-controlled [S3].

The bill takes effect 180 days after enactment without waiting for the Federal Election Commission to write regulations, leaving companies to comply with new tests before formal agency guidance exists [S3].
Enforcement ultimately depends on the FEC, an agency whose structural gridlock has historically limited campaign-finance enforcement; the bill adds rules but no new enforcement mechanism [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — closing a known channel for foreign money in U.S. elections — is significant, and the costs fall mainly on a narrow set of foreign-influenced corporations and their executives, who would face certification paperwork and lost political spending power. The main honest caveats are compliance uncertainty for companies near the ownership thresholds and the fact that the new rules would operate without FEC regulations and through an FEC that has struggled to enforce existing campaign-finance law [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Committee on House Administration the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so the bill died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jamie Raskin introduced the bill on January 24, 2019, joined by Rep. Abigail Spanberger, and it was referred to the House Committee on House Administration the same day [S1].
The bill never advanced beyond that referral: the full action history shows no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action [S5].
It attracted 5 cosponsors, all House Democrats, and no further movement before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies with foreign ownership or influence that spend money in U.S. federal elections — and executives who would otherwise have had to certify compliance under penalty of perjury — are better off because the bill never advanced. Voters gained no new protection, since the gap in the foreign-money ban remains as it was.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Foreign-influenced corporations; no change for voters

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call positions exist; all of its sponsor and 5 cosponsors were Democrats, and the Democratic-run committee that buried it was also controlled by the sponsoring party's majority.

industries.note: These companies would lose the ability to make campaign contributions and expenditures and would have to file annual CEO certifications under penalty of perjury. Their political spending power is exactly what the bill removes from the electoral system.

industries.industry: Super PACs and outside spending groups
industries.note: The bill cuts off disbursements from committees that accept non-compliant donations and conditions corporate PAC money on certifying no foreign participation in decisions. Legitimate groups lose a gray-area funding channel; the public gains a closed laundering route.
